pedagogy.summary: Read time and value axes together to solve line-graph comparison, difference and appropriate sum problems. Separate point height from change across equal time intervals; graph shape is not a literal picture of the situation. Temperature readings support trend interpretation and approximate interpolation under an explicit straight-line model. Period totals, such as monthly rainfall, can be compared and added but cannot be interpolated as rainfall at an intermediate date. Teach literal reads before combining values and interpreting trends.
bestPractices: Anchor the graph in a clear quantity, units and observation schedule; distinguish temperature observations from rainfall totals over periods.

Explicitly teach the three-part reading progression (Curcio): first READ THE DATA (lift a value straight off a point), then READ BETWEEN THE DATA (compare two points, find a difference, read an intermediate value), then READ BEYOND (predict the next day) — and name which you are asking for

Separate HEIGHT from CHANGE deliberately: pair 'which day was warmest?' (height) with 'which day did it warm up the most?' (steepest rise) on the same graph, so children cannot conflate the tallest point with the biggest jump
Trace vertically from a plotted point to the time axis, then horizontally from that same point to the value axis; say the paired reading.
Read an intermediate temperature from the segment as a straight-line estimate; distinguish this model assumption from what was measured.

Contrast a genuine time-series (temperature) with data that should NOT be joined into a line (favourite fruit) so children learn that joined lines suit values ordered in time, such as temperature readings or monthly totals, whereas unordered categories should not be joined
keyRepresentations: Temperature-over-a-week line graph (the canonical continuous time-series for this age)

A crosshair / ruler slid along the line to read plotted values and to estimate values between plotted temperature observations under a straight-line assumption (makes interpolation visible as an estimate)
Paired axes with a right-angle trace from point to time-axis and to value-axis
Two questions side by side on one graph — 'highest point' vs 'steepest climb' — to physically separate height from change
A rising / flat / falling segment triad annotated as increase / no change / decrease
commonMisconceptions: Graph-as-picture: reading the line's silhouette as a literal picture of the situation (a rising-then-falling temperature line 'is a hill/mountain', or a distance-time line read as the route travelled) rather than as a quantity plotted against time

Slope-height / height-for-difference confusion: when asked how much a quantity changed, naming the highest point rather than the steepest segment; treating a higher point as 'faster' or 'more increase'
Treating a line-based estimate as an exact unmeasured observation, or refusing any estimate because only the plotted points were measured.
Accepting or interpreting a joined line for categorical data (favourite pet) as if it showed a trend, or reading a scaled axis by counting squares rather than by the scale interval

learn.summary: For ages 9–10, solve comparison, sum and difference problems from line graphs. Read each point using both axes and the labelled scale; distinguish the highest observed value from the largest increase over equal time intervals. Use temperatures for reading and differences, and quantities that can meaningfully be added, such as monthly rainfall totals, for sum problems. Interpolated temperatures are estimates under a stated straight-line assumption, not additional measurements. Joining monthly rainfall totals does not reveal rainfall on intermediate dates.

activities.title: Read values and estimate between temperature observations
feedback: If you tap the tallest point for 'warmed up the most', that tells you the warmest day, which may or may not be where the biggest change happened — look instead for the segment that climbs most steeply across a single day.

If you read a value without tracing to both axes, pause: put your finger on the point, go straight down to read the day, then from the point go straight across to read the temperature, and say the pair.

The drawn segment passes smoothly through in-between values. Those are estimates assuming a straight-line change between readings; actual temperatures may have fluctuated differently, so this is not a record of every intervening temperature.
activities.rationale: Reading a time-series is a doing skill — lift a value, read between two values, find a difference, interpret a rise. Letting the learner act and the graph respond is intended to make interpolation and the slope-vs-height distinction concrete. A draggable/sliding read-out is one proposed way that may make the continuity of the segment visible; a ruler slid along a printed graph achieves a similar effect. Efficacy of the specific interaction is untested here.
sourceClaims: Slope-height confusion and related substitutions (height-for-slope, slope-for-height, height-for-difference, slope-for-curvature): students use the wrong graphical feature for the quantity asked; McDermott et al. found as many as half of students used height instead of slope to judge speed

KS2 line-graph teaching: line graphs are used for continuous data where points between plotted points carry meaning; a rising line means an increase, a falling line a decrease, a flat line no change; pupils read values and find differences from the graph
learnerActions: Use a temperature-over-a-week line graph with observations at the same time each day and equal daily spacing. Slide a ruler, crosshair or finger along a segment to read a straight-line estimate between observations.

Slide between Monday and Tuesday and say aloud the values the line passes through — e.g. 14, 15, 16 degrees — noticing that the line gives estimated in-between values, not only the measured values at the plotted dots.

For each point, trace it back to BOTH axes: finger on the point, drop straight down to the time axis to read the day, then go back to the point and slide horizontally across to the value axis to read the temperature; say the paired coordinate.
Use a 'find the difference' move: mark two points and read the vertical gap between them (e.g. the rise from Tuesday to Wednesday).
Take on the challenge 'Which day did it warm up the MOST?' — then check whether the warmest day (tallest point) is the same as, or different from, the day of the steepest climb.
activities.intendedInsight: On this temperature graph, plotted points are observations and the connecting segments provide straight-line estimates between them. Compare rises over equal daily intervals to distinguish change from the temperature at a point.

activities.title: Separate HEIGHT from CHANGE on one graph
feedback: If you name the warmest day for 'warmed up the most', check the arrows — the longest upward arrow marks the biggest rise, which may not sit at the tallest point.
Correct justification sounds like 'it climbed 5 degrees from Monday to Tuesday', not 'that one is the highest'.
If height and steepest always seem to be the same day for you, try the tricky case where they come apart.
activities.rationale: Pairing a height question with a change question on the same graph targets height-for-difference confusion, a documented substitution error; comparing arrow lengths makes 'how much it changed' a visible, measurable quantity distinct from the tallest point.
sourceClaims: Slope-height confusion and related substitutions (height-for-slope, slope-for-height, height-for-difference, slope-for-curvature): students use the wrong graphical feature for the quantity asked; McDermott et al. found as many as half of students used height instead of slope to judge speed
learnerActions: On a single temperature line graph, answer 'Which day was warmest?' (height) and 'Which day did it warm up the most?' (steepest rise) — treat them as two different questions.
Draw a small vertical arrow for the change between each pair of consecutive days, pointing up for a rise and down for a fall, then compare the lengths of the upward arrows to find the biggest rise.
Justify your 'warmed up the most' answer by saying how far the line climbed across that one day, not by which point is highest.

Try a tricky case: a graph where a huge jump happens early in the week and the highest point is reached later by only a small rise, so the tallest point and the steepest segment are clearly on different days — identify each.
activities.intendedInsight: A higher observed temperature is not the same as a bigger increase. Over these equal one-day intervals, the largest rise has the steepest rising segment; with unequal intervals, compare changes and rates separately.

activities.title: Read the data, between the data, and beyond the data
feedback: For a difference question, report the gap (e.g. rose 3 degrees), not the two raw values; for a total/sum question, add the two read-off values and report the combined amount.

An intermediate point on the drawn temperature segment gives a straight-line estimate. Read it consistently with the axes and explain that the actual unmeasured value could differ; an exactly known temperature cannot be recovered from two daily observations alone.
A prediction is a reasoned guess from the trend; being off from the revealed value is fine — explain what the trend suggested.
activities.rationale: Curcio's three hierarchical levels structure the questions from literal lift to comparing/combining/finding differences to inference; this is where comparison, sum and difference problems from the graph live. Predict-then-reveal exercises reading beyond the data and makes the continuity of the line matter.
sourceClaims: Curcio's three hierarchical levels of graph comprehension — reading the data (literal lift), reading between the data (compare/combine/find differences), reading beyond the data (predict/infer) — students must read the data before they can read between or beyond it; framework adopted by NCTM for assessment

KS2 line-graph teaching: line graphs are used for continuous data where points between plotted points carry meaning; a rising line means an increase, a falling line a decrease, a flat line no change; pupils read values and find differences from the graph
learnerActions: Read the data: lift a single value straight off a marked point (e.g. the warmest day's temperature).

Read between the data: compare two observed values, find their difference, and combine values only where the quantity makes a meaningful total, such as rainfall totals for March and May. Do not add daily temperatures as if they were a total temperature. On a temperature line graph, separately estimate an intermediate value under the straight-line assumption.

Read beyond the data: hide the final plotted day (e.g. Friday on a Monday-to-Friday graph), predict and place it from the earlier trend, then reveal the real value and compare — discuss why the prediction may differ.
Each time, name which kind of reading you are doing: reading a value, reading between, or predicting.
activities.intendedInsight: Graph comprehension has a progression — you must read a value before you can compare, combine or find differences between values, and only then predict or infer — and naming which you are doing clarifies the task.

activities.title: When should data be joined into a line? Continuous vs categorical
feedback: A point between two temperature observations has a time and a line-based estimate. The true temperature at that time was not measured by this graph and need not match the estimate.
If you would join favourite-fruit counts with a line, ask: what would a point halfway between apple and banana mean? There is no in-between fruit category — so the counts should not be joined.
activities.rationale: Contrasting temperature observations with unordered categorical counts may help learners explain when joining points supports a meaningful interpretation. Temperature interpolation remains a model-based estimate; this proposed comparison is not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: KS2 line-graph teaching: line graphs are used for continuous data where points between plotted points carry meaning; a rising line means an increase, a falling line a decrease, a flat line no change; pupils read values and find differences from the graph
learnerActions: Compare a genuine time-series (temperature across days) with categorical data (favourite fruit) and decide which should be drawn as a joined line and which should not.
Run a finger along a temperature segment, naming the estimates it passes through ('the line estimates about 15 here'); distinguish these from temperatures actually measured at the plotted points.
Explain why joining 'favourite fruit' counts into a line would be meaningless — there is no continuous quantity between the categories.
activities.intendedInsight: A line joining temperature observations can show a trend and support estimates under an explicit interpolation assumption. Joining unordered fruit categories does not create a meaningful intermediate category; use bars for those counts.

activities.title: Confront the graph-as-picture habit
feedback: Describing the silhouette ('it went up and over') is the picture trap — switch to values: 'on Wednesday it was 18, on Thursday it fell to 14'.
A falling segment means the quantity decreased (it got colder), not that something physically went downhill.
activities.rationale: The graph-as-picture error persists even when a learner can describe the changes verbally, so directly re-reading point-by-point and tracing to axes aims to break the habit of treating the silhouette as the situation.
sourceClaims: Graph-as-picture error: students treat the graph as a literal picture of the problem situation (drawing/reading a hill shape for a speed-vs-time graph over a hill), with two subtypes — global correspondence (whole scene matched to whole graph) and feature correspondence (a local visual feature matched to a graph feature); this occurs even when the student can describe the changes verbally
learnerActions: If you catch yourself describing the line as 'a hill' or 'the route it travelled', cover the whole line and expose one point at a time.
For each exposed point, answer 'What does THIS point tell us?' and trace it to both axes, reading a day and its temperature.
Re-read the whole graph as a set of day/temperature pairs rather than a shape or a scene.
activities.intendedInsight: The line is a quantity plotted against time, not a literal picture of the event; each point is a paired coordinate, and the overall shape summarises how the value changed, not a landscape.

activities.title: Check questions and reading the scale correctly
feedback: If your answer is off by a consistent factor (e.g. you say 6 where each square is 2 degrees and the real answer is 12), you counted squares instead of using the scale — relabel the interval and re-read.

The highest temperature and largest one-day rise can occur together or on different days. Compare consecutive values over equal daily intervals before deciding; do not automatically reject the highest point.
activities.rationale: Comparison, difference, sum and ordering questions give a scorable check of the reading procedure, but recognition alone does not elicit the learner's own interpolation or justification, so keep producing-and-explaining tasks too. Scale mis-reading is a counting slip, not a conceptual gap, and is addressed by labelling the scale interval first. Any illustration should be schematic rather than requiring an exact drawn quantity to be eyeballed.
sourceClaims: Curcio's three hierarchical levels of graph comprehension — reading the data (literal lift), reading between the data (compare/combine/find differences), reading beyond the data (predict/infer) — students must read the data before they can read between or beyond it; framework adopted by NCTM for assessment
learnerActions: Answer scorable items: choose the warmest day; estimate an intermediate temperature off a marked line (a sensible range is accepted); fill in 'the difference between March and May rainfall is ___ mm'; order months by rainfall.
Include one item that pairs 'highest point' against 'biggest rise' so you must distinguish height from change.
Before reporting any value, ask 'How much is each square worth here?' and label the scale interval, then read by the scale — not by counting squares as if each were one unit.
activities.intendedInsight: Targeted questions can check your reading skill, but you must read values by the axis scale interval, not by counting grid squares.

constraints: This topic assesses reading and solving problems from line graphs. Constructing a complete graph is developed separately in the later Line graphs topic (mt_HlNSurPVDp); do not require unrelated bar-chart tasks as evidence of this objective.

Always trace values back to BOTH axes (from the point, go vertically to the time axis to read the time, and horizontally from the point to the value axis to read the value) to counter reading the line as a shape rather than paired coordinates.

Deliberately pair a height question ('which day was warmest?') with a change question ('which day warmed up the most?') on the same graph so learners cannot conflate the tallest point with the biggest jump.

For temperature observations joined by straight segments, read intermediate estimates aloud and name the straight-line assumption. The line does not establish the exact path taken between observations. Do not interpolate monthly rainfall totals as rainfall on intermediate dates.

A labelled or tap-to-reveal graph can support a worked example. Ask the learner to read and explain new values before revealing answers when independent reading is the aim; paper tracing, discussion and digital controls are optional ways to organize this.

Recognition-only or pre-revealed items can confirm a classification or choice but do not themselves elicit the learner's own reading, difference-finding, combining/totalling, interpolation, or justification; include tasks where the learner produces and explains answers.
Scorable check items should use schematic illustrations and must not require eyeballing an exact drawn quantity that isn't readable from the scale.
Scale mis-reading is a counting slip to scaffold (label the interval, re-read), not a reason to reteach the whole graph concept.

For unordered categories such as favourite fruit, use bars rather than a joined trend line. Line graphs can also plot ordered period totals, but joining monthly totals does not supply rainfall amounts at intervening dates.

Where a point-only (intermediate-values-don't-exist) misconception appears, reteaching the continuous meaning may draw on the prerequisite micro-topic (continuous vs categorical data) rather than re-teaching the whole graph idea.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels conversation/persona and 3D treatments as poor fits, asserting a third spatial dimension 'conveys nothing' and that a conversational wrapper 'could not verify' reading. These are catalog-style comparative claims not established by the cited sources and are omitted as universal laws. Narrowly scoped, observable concerns remain worth noting: a time-series is a two-variable (time vs quantity) plot, so an added spatial dimension does not correspond to a variable here and may invite the graph-as-picture error; and a purely decorative conversational wrapper would still need a live graph to check reading. These are affordance observations, not proof that any medium 'cannot teach'.
The original feedback marked the tallest point wrong for biggest rise. This is not generally valid: the highest temperature and largest rise may coincide, so each graph must be checked.
One cited source (Oak National Academy KS2 line-graph guidance) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claim as curriculum guidance of unconfirmed verification.

Draggable crosshair, live recolouring (steepest segment lighting up), and predict-then-drag are optional interaction examples that may make continuity and the height-vs-change distinction concrete; paper equivalents (sliding a ruler, drawing arrows) are acceptable, and these specific interactions are not required or proven mechanisms.
The original summary and evidence include SUM/total problems; a combine/total task was added to the read-between activity so this is genuinely delivered rather than only promised.
Taxonomy alignment repair after os-taxonomy PR #30 (2026-10-19). Sources were reused without being re-fetched. Activities are proposals, not empirically validated interventions.
The temporary bar-graph activities introduced to match the former description have been removed. PR #30 corrected the description to match the original line-graph evidence and assessment.

probeDeeper: Why is Friday warmest even though Monday–Tuesday has the biggest rise?
Could the actual temperature halfway between observations differ from 17°C? Explain the assumption behind the estimate.
Why can January and March rainfall totals be added, while daily temperatures are not a total temperature?
How would a value axis marked every 2°C change the way you read a point?
assess.correctAnswer: Friday is warmest at 19°C; Tuesday to Wednesday rises by 2°C; Monday to Tuesday has the largest daily rise, 4°C, although Friday is highest. Halfway between Tuesday noon and Wednesday noon the straight-line estimate is 17°C; the actual unmeasured temperature may differ. January plus March rainfall is 45 mm and February exceeds January by 15 mm. Wednesday to Thursday falls by 1°C, meaning the temperature decreased (it got colder), not that something went downhill. Both traces start at the plotted point: vertically to time and horizontally to value. Do not total daily temperatures or interpolate monthly rainfall totals as rainfall at an intermediate date.

errorPatterns.pattern: Graph-as-picture: reads the line's shape as a literal picture of the situation rather than a quantity over time ('it goes up like a hill then down the other side', or describes it as a route/mountain) instead of talking about temperature values on days
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront directly: cover the whole line and expose one point at a time, asking 'what does THIS point tell us?' and tracing it to both axes, until the child re-reads the line as a set of day/temperature pairs rather than a picture
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (6), or whenever asked to explain the line, the child narrates the silhouette ('it went up and over') and gestures the shape, rather than tying height at each day to a temperature value

errorPatterns.pattern: Height-for-difference (slope-height confusion): when asked how much the quantity CHANGED, names the highest point rather than the steepest segment; treats a higher point as 'more increase' or 'faster'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront by putting 'highest point' and 'biggest jump' side by side on the same graph: mark the change between each pair of consecutive days with a little vertical arrow, and compare arrow lengths so the steepest rise is seen to differ from the tallest point
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (3) the child points to the warmest day (same point as task 1) and says 'that one, it's the highest', instead of the day with the biggest jump from the day before

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses observed values with line-based estimates: either asserts an exact unmeasured temperature or cannot make an estimate even when the straight-line assumption is explicitly supplied.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate plotted observations from model estimates; mark the halfway position, read 17°C on the straight segment and explain that real temperatures could have varied differently.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Claims 17°C is a known observation, or refuses a line-based estimate after the interpolation assumption is made explicit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Scale mis-read: on task (1) or (2) counts grid squares as if each were one unit instead of reading the scale interval, giving a value or difference that is off by the scale factor
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, do not reteach the graph idea: ask 'how much is each square worth here?' and have them label the scale interval before re-reading; the interpretation is sound, only the counting slipped
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child locates the correct point and the correct pair, but the number they report is wrong by the scale factor (e.g. says 6 where each square is 2 degrees and the answer is 12)

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably read the axes or distinguishes neither point height nor daily change.
responseLevels.full: Reads values by the scale, distinguishes highest from largest rise, solves the rainfall sum/difference, explains a falling segment as a decrease in temperature and explains interpolation as an assumption-based estimate; transfers the procedure to another graph.
responseLevels.partial: Reads observed values and finds a difference, but needs support to compare increases, explain an estimate or select quantities that can be added.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give an equally spaced line graph of temperatures recorded at noon: Monday 12°C, Tuesday 16°C, Wednesday 18°C, Thursday 17°C, Friday 19°C. Ask the learner to (1) read the warmest day and value, (2) calculate the Tuesday-to-Wednesday change, and (3) identify the interval with the largest rise. (4) Ask for the estimated temperature halfway between Tuesday noon and Wednesday noon, explicitly assuming straight-line change. (5) Then show a line graph of monthly rainfall totals (January 20 mm, February 35 mm, March 25 mm); ask for January plus March and the February–January difference. (6) Return to the temperature graph and ask what the falling Wednesday-to-Thursday segment means. Watch the reading and calculations without supplying the answers.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The fixed data deliberately separate the highest point (Friday) from the largest rise (Monday–Tuesday). Watching axis traces, scale reading and subtraction distinguishes sound graph reading from guessing by shape. The estimate requires an explicit assumption; a learner is not marked wrong for adding that the exact unmeasured value is unknown, provided they give the 17°C straight-line estimate. The rainfall questions check a meaningful sum and difference, and explaining the Wednesday-to-Thursday fall checks that a falling segment is read as a decrease rather than a picture.
